extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (novelists and short-story writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for creating, revising, and polishing fiction — especially novels and longer short fiction: character development, symbolism, theme, drafting workflow, and revision habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters determined by the story (the 'fossil' approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The characters of my protagonist and antagonist were determined by the story I had to tell — by the fossil, the found object, in other words.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure fictional people behave in ways that will both help the story and seem reasonable to us given what we know about them (and real life). Let the story/found object dictate character choices rather than forcing characters that don't fit; characters often reveal self-doubt or pity, and if you do your job they will 'come to life and start doing stuff on their own.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make protagonists likable through ordinary, relatable detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an average or potentially problematic protagonist vivid and likable by showing ordinary, sympathetic behaviors (e.g., taking a girl to the county fair, being sincerely in love, principled sexual restraint balanced with humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use everyday scenes and small acts (returning a lost wallet, helping with a flat tire) to build reader sympathy without turning the character into a 'plaster saint.' Balance principles with humanizing quirks so the reader will 'become our friend' with the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Villain authenticity and persuasive charm
rubrics_metrics.description: Villains should be authentically nasty and genuinely frightening, not merely cartoonish evil; they must also be persuasive and able to 'camouflage' themselves socially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish menace early (example: Stillson teargassing and kicking a dog when alone) so the reader understands the danger. Make readers think, 'This guy is out of control—how come somebody can't see through him?' The villain's charm/skill at camouflage increases the story stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of small symbolic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Small details (a glow-in-the-dark Halloween mask, initials like J.C., recurring blood images) can work as symbols and enrich a story when they arise naturally from the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolism often appears in revision rather than by conscious design; if you notice symbolic threads, 'polish it until it shines' and cut it like a jeweler would. Use such details to focus and unify the work, but only when they truly belong to the 'fossil' of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism should adorn and enrich, not create artificial profundity
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism exists to adorn and enrich; it should summarize and encapsulate meaning but not be used to manufacture fake depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If symbolism is present, bring it out carefully; if it isn't, leave well enough alone. Avoid getting carried away—overused or forced symbolism can hurt the story. Treat symbolism as another kind of figurative language and a focusing device for you and your reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with story; derive and clarify theme in revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Good fiction 'always begins with story and progresses to theme'; one should not begin with theme (except for certain allegories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the basic story first and only afterward ask 'what's it all about?' Use the second draft to make the theme clearer — this produces focus and a more unified story. Theme is a tool to be applied after the story is on paper, not a starting blueprint (with the possible exception of explicit allegory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use any stylistic device only if it improves the story; be willing to delete
rubrics_metrics.description: All bells and whistles—onomatopoeia, incremental repetition, stream of consciousness, tense changes, alliteration—are available to you, but you should use anything that improves the quality of writing and doesn’t get in the way of your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a phrase or device 'seems to work, it can stay. If it doesn't ... that DELETE key is on your machine for a good reason.' 'Murder your darlings'—toss beloved passages that don't serve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and honesty; transcribe clearly and avoid unnecessary adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice is invaluable and 'honesty is indispensable.' Skills in description, dialogue, and character development boil down to seeing or hearing clearly and transcribing it with equal clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clear, honest transcription of sensory detail and dialogue; avoid 'a lot of tiresome, unnecessary adverbs.' Regular practice should feel good and not like aimless drills.

rubrics_metrics.name: First draft: All-Story Draft (door shut) — write rapidly and privately
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the first draft (the 'All-Story Draft') with the door shut, downloading what's in your head as fast as comfortable, looking back only for names and backstory checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist showing the first draft to anyone (even close friends or partners) because external praise or doubt can derail focus; writing rapidly helps outrun self-doubt and keeps you concentrated on telling the story rather than being 'wonderful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision workflow: two drafts and a polish (door open for later drafts)
rubrics_metrics.description: King's routine: two drafts and a polish (and with word-processing that polish may approach a third draft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the All-Story Draft (door shut) let the manuscript rest, then do a second draft with the door open (sharing and revising), and finish with a polish to clean prose and details. Use the second draft to bring out patterns, symbolism, and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the manuscript rest (minimum six weeks) before revising
rubrics_metrics.description: After finishing the first draft, put the manuscript away for a period (minimum of six weeks) so it can 'age' and mellow while you work on something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During this rest period resist the temptation to re-read or tinker; come back when the manuscript seems like an alien relic and you can read it with fresh eyes. Doing something different (shorter work or daily life) helps you return with perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: First draft is the wrong place to analyze symbolism or theme
rubrics_metrics.description: The first draft should concentrate on story to the exclusion of almost everything else; it is the wrong place to think about symbolism or the significance of details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asking meta-questions while drafting (e.g., 'What does the green dress mean?'); reserve thematic and symbolic analysis for revision when you can 'step back and look at the forest.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the manuscript in one sitting and fix housekeeping errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When ready to revise, read the manuscript over (in one sitting if possible) and make notes, concentrating on mundane housekeeping: misspellings and inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There will be plenty of small errors; fix them rather than relying entirely on copyeditors. Make comprehensive notes and prioritize clarity and internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thematic thinking as a practical tool to solve structural problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking 'what is this book about?' can lead to revelations that solve narrative jams (example: The Stand’s bomb-in-the-closet revelation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thematic thinking is not just academic—use it to find fixes and to unify sprawling narratives. If stuck, step back and ask why you started and what the story ultimately means; the answer often points to structural solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural devices (epistolary interludes, multiple perspectives) only when they serve the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural choices such as epistolary interludes or shifting-perspective narratives can inject realism or solve length/pace issues (example: Carrie’s epistolary passages; The Stand’s shifting-perspective sections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose such devices because they enhance realism, pacing, or narrative needs, not because they are fashionable. If the first draft is too short or feels like it needs realism, an epistolary frame may help; if a multi-character epic is intended, ensure the structure links characters meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be reasonably reader-friendly before sending work out
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't allow a story or novel outside your study unless you feel it's 'reasonably reader-friendly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can't please every reader, but you should aim to please at least some. Judge your work and polish it until you feel confident about its readability before seeking external feedback or submission.
